standard.title: Significant individuals in Asia-Pacific
standard.description: the role and achievements of a significant individual and/or group in the Asian-Pacific society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain the role and achievements of significant individuals in ancient and imperial contexts (AC9HH7K13, AC9HH8K05, AC9HH8K10). They understand the social and cultural features of the chosen Asia-Pacific society (AC9HH8K12). They have not yet applied significance analysis to individuals specifically connected to Asia-Pacific societies — Khmer rulers, Japanese shoguns, or Polynesian groups.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the role and achievements of a significant individual or group in the chosen Asia-Pacific society — describing what they did, the conditions that enabled their actions, and the impact and legacy of their achievements.

nodes.label: Role and context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the role of the chosen individual or group in their Asia-Pacific society and explain the conditions that enabled their significance.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of the chosen individual or group's role with reference to the historical conditions that enabled it.
nodes.typical_width: The chosen individual or group situated within their society's context. Examples: Jayavarman VII — his rule, expansion of the Khmer Empire, expulsion of the Chams, and the scale of the Angkor construction program; Tokugawa Ieyasu as founder of the Edo Shogunate — the conditions that enabled his consolidation of power; Polynesian groups (Māori, Samoan, Tahitian, Tongan, Rapa Nui) and their achievements in settlement, navigation and cultural development.
wider: For the Khmer: examine Jayavarman VII's rule as both military leader (expelling the Chams) and builder (Angkor's construction program) — and consider whether these two roles were connected or in tension

For Polynesia: compare the achievements of different Polynesian groups across navigation, settlement and cultural development to understand how similar social structures and technologies enabled diverse achievements across the Pacific

response_modes.reason: Students need to contextualise the individual or group's role before assessing their achievements. Scaffold the question: what conditions made this person's or group's actions possible, and why were they positioned to act as they did?

success_criteria: Describes the role of the chosen individual or group in their Asia-Pacific society
Identifies at least one condition that enabled their significance

nodes.label: Achievements and impact
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the key achievements of the chosen individual or group and describe their impact on the society and on later developments.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two achievements with an explanation of their impact on the society.
nodes.typical_width: Multiple achievements analysed for immediate and longer-term impact. Examples: Jayavarman VII's expansion of the Khmer Empire and construction program; the legacy of Tokugawa Ieyasu in establishing the Edo Shogunate and Japan's subsequent isolation; the achievements of Polynesian peoples in navigation, settlement of diverse island environments, development of distinctive cultures and resource management practices.
wider: For the Khmer: examine the influence of Jayavarman VII's building program on both the empire's power and its later fragility — asking whether great achievement can also contain the seeds of decline

For Polynesia: describe the achievements of one Polynesian group — their navigation techniques, settlement strategies, cultural innovations — and evaluate what these achievements reveal about the capabilities and values of Pacific peoples
nodes.hinge_reason: Achievement analysis is the core demand of this descriptor. Students who narrate events rather than explaining achievements and impacts have not met the standard. Legacy analysis depends on solid achievement analysis here.

response_modes.reason: Students often describe what a ruler did without connecting it to impact. Scaffold the distinction: an achievement is not an event but a consequential act. Each achievement needs an explanation of what it changed or enabled for the society.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two achievements of the chosen individual or group
Explains the impact of at least one achievement on the society and on later developments

nodes.label: Legacy and significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the legacy of the chosen individual or group — explaining what endured from their achievements and how historians or cultural traditions have assessed their significance.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of at least one lasting legacy and a reference to how the individual or group is regarded in historical or cultural memory.
nodes.typical_width: Legacy evaluated across multiple criteria; connections to subsequent historical developments; the relationship between historical judgement and cultural memory. Examples: Tokugawa Ieyasu's legacy in shaping Japan's political culture and later modernisation; the enduring cultural achievements of Polynesian peoples including navigational knowledge, oral traditions and material culture; the architectural legacy of Angkor Wat as a UNESCO World Heritage site.
wider: For Polynesia: examine how the achievements of Polynesian peoples — particularly their navigational knowledge and settlement of the Pacific — have been recognised and reclaimed in contemporary cultural and political contexts

For the Khmer: consider how Angkor Wat's significance as a World Heritage site reflects both the enduring achievement of Jayavarman VII and the contemporary importance of cultural heritage to Cambodian identity

response_modes.reason: Legacy assessment integrates contextual understanding (Node 1) and achievement analysis (Node 2). Invest in helping students move from describing what was achieved to evaluating what endured and why it continues to matter.

success_criteria: Explains at least one lasting legacy of the chosen individual or group
Connects the legacy to the society's longer-term history or to contemporary significance
